title: Neon vs Supabase
description: A technical comparison of Neon and Supabase for hosted Postgres workloads in 2026. Covers architecture, branching, autoscaling, connection pooling, replication, pricing, and the backend services each one now ships around Postgres.
introduction:
If you want managed Postgres without standing up RDS yourself, Neon and Supabase are the two names that come up first. They look superficially similar. Both run Postgres, both have generous free tiers, both ship branching, both index pgvector for AI workloads, and since September 2026 both bundle auth, object storage, and functions with the database. Underneath, they are very different products solving very different problems.

Neon is a complete backend built on Lakebase Postgres, its serverless Postgres. The team rebuilt the bottom half of Postgres in Rust so that compute and storage can scale independently, then wrapped it in a control plane that exposes branching, autoscaling, and scale-to-zero as first-class primitives. It looks like Postgres to your application. Same wire protocol, same extensions, same SQL. But every dial that used to require operations work (provisioning, vacuuming pages off hot disks, building read replicas, restoring from a snapshot) is now a metadata operation. Databricks acquired Neon in 2025 and used the headroom to drop storage prices from $1.75 to $0.35 per GB-month, cut compute rates, and double the free tier's compute allowance. In June 2026 Neon added Object Storage, Functions, and an AI Gateway around the database, and on 17 September 2026 those, together with Managed Better Auth (the Better Auth-based rebuild of Neon Auth), became generally available. Realtime followed as a public beta in October 2026. Each branch carries its own copy of that backend, so a preview gets its own data, files, and users. The same architecture powers Databricks' Lakebase. The 2026 cadence has been heavy on AI-agent tooling. Claimable Neon (the account-free database formerly called Neon Launchpad) provisions a new database in about two seconds without an account, and `neon init` wires up Claude Code, Cursor, and VS Code directly, with MCP flows for Codex, Cline, Zed, and most other AI assistants in the wild.

Supabase is a backend-as-a-service built around a regular Postgres instance. Each project gets a dedicated Postgres VM plus a stack of services on top: PostgREST for an instant REST API, Supabase Auth (which started life as a GoTrue fork), a Realtime server for websocket subscriptions, an S3-compatible Storage gateway, Supavisor for connection pooling, and Edge Functions on a Deno-compatible runtime for serverless logic. The marketing line is "open-source Firebase alternative," and that framing is accurate. You trade some database-level control for a batteries-included backend that can ship a working product in a weekend. The platform is moving fast too: a $500M raise in June 2026 at a $10.5B valuation, a preview of Multigres for Vitess-style horizontal scaling, and a security overhaul that stopped auto-exposing database tables through the Data API on new projects.

The choice is rarely "Postgres vs Postgres." Both now bundle a backend; the difference is how it is built, how mature each piece is, and what it costs as you add previews, users, and projects. This comparison walks through the dimensions that actually matter when picking between them: how branching works at the storage layer, what scale-to-zero means for your bill, where the connection pooling lives, and which platform handles the long tail of database operations (PITR, replicas, version coverage) without forcing you off the happy path. Prices and plan limits on this page were checked against both vendors' live pricing pages and docs on 23 November 2026.

toolA.name: Neon
toolA.description: A complete backend built on Lakebase Postgres, with separated compute and storage. Branching is copy-on-write at the storage layer, autoscaling is built in, and idle databases scale to zero. Managed Better Auth, Object Storage, Functions, an AI Gateway, the Data API, and Realtime (public beta) sit next to the database and branch with it.
pros: Copy-on-write branching at the storage layer creates a full data branch in milliseconds regardless of database size
Scale-to-zero on idle and autoscaling between 0.25 and 16 CU mean you only pay for the compute you actually use
Custom Rust storage engine (Pageservers + Safekeepers) decouples compute restarts from data durability and restores to any timestamp or LSN in seconds
Postgres 14 through 19, with 18 the default for new projects. The broadest version coverage among managed serverless Postgres providers
Native serverless driver over WebSockets removes TCP setup cost on Vercel Functions, Cloudflare Workers, and other edge runtimes
Read replicas are first-class compute endpoints that share storage with the primary, so adding one is an API call rather than a streaming-replication setup
Postgres-native: every wire-protocol client, ORM, migration tool, and extension that runs on vanilla Postgres works without special drivers

Managed Better Auth ships authentication with users in the neon_auth schema, isolated per branch, queryable via SQL and RLS, and included up to 1M monthly active users per project on paid plans (60K on Free)
The whole backend branches: a branch gets its own Object Storage buckets, Functions, and auth users, so a preview environment is a copy of the backend, not just the database
cons: The backend services are younger than Supabase's: Object Storage, Functions, the AI Gateway, and Managed Better Auth went GA in September 2026, Realtime is a public beta since October 2026, and Functions, Object Storage, the AI Gateway, and Realtime run in four of Neon's eight AWS regions so far
Cold-start latency on scale-to-zero compute is typically 300-500 ms, which matters for the very first request after an idle window
Compute sizes above 16 CU are fixed-size (no autoscaling), so the largest workloads still need manual capacity planning
Some Postgres extensions take longer to land than on a self-managed instance because they have to be vetted against the Pageserver
Smaller community than Supabase for application-layer recipes and mobile SDKs, and Functions are not a job queue: queued, retryable work still needs a queue such as Inngest or Upstash QStash

toolB.name: Supabase
toolB.description: An open-source backend-as-a-service built around a dedicated Postgres instance. Bundles PostgREST APIs, Supabase Auth, a Realtime server, S3-compatible storage, Supavisor pooling, and Deno-based Edge Functions in one platform.
pros: Bundles authentication, REST/GraphQL, realtime subscriptions, storage, and edge functions so a small team can ship a backend without integrating multiple vendors
Row Level Security policies move authorization into the database, which is powerful in practice when designed for from day one
Supavisor (Elixir-based pooler, benchmarked to 1M connections cluster-wide) ships on every project, with per-project client limits scaling from 200 on Micro to 12,000 on the largest compute
Generated TypeScript types from the live schema make end-to-end type safety nearly free
Local development environment runs the full stack in Docker so you can prototype offline
Active community of templates and starter apps for common product shapes (B2B SaaS, marketplaces, mobile apps)

Active platform iteration: PostgREST v14's JWT cache added roughly 20% more throughput on authenticated GETs, Analytics Buckets (Apache Iceberg) and Supabase ETL are in alpha for analytics workloads, and Multigres previews Vitess-style horizontal scaling
cons: Branching provisions a brand-new Postgres instance per branch. Branching 2.0 dropped the Git requirement, but branches still copy schema and config only, starting with empty data unless you supply a seed script
Free-tier projects auto-pause after 7 days of inactivity, which makes the free plan unsuitable for low-traffic production workloads
Each project is a dedicated Postgres VM, so compute cannot scale to zero and idle projects keep accruing the base compute charge

Pro ($25/month per organization) includes only $10 of compute credits; each project bills its own compute from $10/month, and metered overage (MAU at $0.00325 above the included 100K, egress, storage) can quickly outrun the headline figure
More moving parts in the stack (Realtime, Auth, Storage, PostgREST) means more services to reason about during incidents, the trade-off for getting them out of the box

useCases.scenario: Vercel or Cloudflare Workers app that needs Postgres with low cold-start latency from the edge
useCases.explanation: Neon's WebSocket-based serverless driver was designed for this workload. It keeps compute warm during traffic, scales to zero between bursts, and the native driver avoids the per-request TCP/TLS setup that dominates latency from edge runtimes. Pricing tracks actual usage rather than a fixed per-project charge, which compounds across preview deployments.

useCases.scenario: CI pipeline that wants a fresh, fully-populated database per pull request and ephemeral preview environment
useCases.explanation: Branching is the load-bearing feature here. Neon's copy-on-write semantics create a writable branch with the parent's full dataset in under a second regardless of size, run the test or preview against it, then garbage-collect the diverged pages when the PR closes. Supabase branches copy schema and config but start without production data, which makes integration tests against production-like datasets harder unless you maintain seed scripts.

useCases.scenario: B2C consumer product that needs auth, storage, file uploads, and realtime presence on day one
useCases.explanation: Both bundles shorten time-to-launch when you'd otherwise be wiring up Auth0, S3, Pusher, and PostgREST yourself. Supabase's is the longer-running one, with mobile SDKs and a Realtime server that is out of beta. Neon's pieces branch with the database, and Managed Better Auth has no per-MAU meter up to 1M users, which matters once a consumer product grows past the 100K MAU included in Supabase Pro. For a small team that needs presence on day one, Supabase is the safer pick today.

useCases.scenario: Background-worker product with bursty Sidekiq/BullMQ traffic and long idle stretches overnight
useCases.explanation: Scale-to-zero is the only mechanism that makes these workloads cheap. A 2-CU Neon compute that handles a daily burst and idles the rest of the time costs a fraction of a Supabase Pro project running a Small instance 24/7, even before counting storage savings.

useCases.scenario: Mobile app with thousands of simultaneous WebSocket connections subscribing to row changes
useCases.explanation: Supabase Realtime is purpose-built for this and has been in production for years, with auth-aware filtering against RLS policies. Neon Realtime, a public beta since October 2026, lets clients subscribe to a SQL query, but for a product that lives on thousands of concurrent row subscriptions the established service is the lower-risk choice.

useCases.scenario: RAG pipeline storing tens of millions of embeddings with sparse, spiky retrieval traffic
useCases.explanation: pgvector works well on both. Neon wins on cost because the compute scales down when retrieval is idle, then ramps to 16 CU when a batch indexing job kicks off. On a fixed-size Supabase instance you provision for the spike and pay for it all month.

useCases.scenario: AI agent or autonomous tool that needs to spin up disposable test databases with specific seed data
useCases.explanation: Neon ships specifically for this loop. Claimable Neon provisions a brand-new database in about two seconds without an account, agent skills let an assistant claim one autonomously, and `neon init` integrates with Claude Code, Cursor, and VS Code directly plus MCP flows for Codex, Cline, Zed, and most other AI assistants. Branching from a known-good parent database in milliseconds is the same primitive used to reset state between runs. Migration-based provisioning is too slow for an agent loop.

useCases.scenario: Existing app with a complex schema and hundreds of migrations moving from RDS to a managed serverless option
useCases.explanation: Postgres-native compatibility matters most here. Neon supports Postgres 14-19 and accepts the same migrations, extensions, and ORM configurations as RDS. Supabase imposes a coupled Auth/Realtime/Storage stack that may conflict with your existing application-layer choices.

useCases.scenario: Internal admin tool or back-office app that wants instant REST and GraphQL APIs over a schema
useCases.explanation: PostgREST and pg_graphql come with Supabase (on new projects you grant table access explicitly and flip pg_graphql on, a one-time setup since the May 2026 security changes), and the auto-generated TypeScript types make a typed admin UI nearly drop-in. Neon's Data API gives you PostgREST-compatible REST over the same schema; for GraphQL and generated admin types you'd add a piece yourself.

useCases.scenario: Mobile-first product where the iOS, Android, and React Native SDK story matters as much as the database
useCases.explanation: Supabase ships well-tested mobile SDKs that bundle auth, realtime, and storage in one client. Neon's backend works from a mobile app through Managed Better Auth, the Data API, and Functions, but you'll be doing more of the client SDK integration work yourself.

faqs.question: Is Neon really just Postgres, or are there compatibility caveats?
faqs.answer: It is real Postgres at the wire-protocol level: same SQL, same JDBC/psycopg/pgx drivers, same migration tools, same ORMs. The compatibility caveats are around extensions: a small number of extensions that depend on writing to local disk (file_fdw, certain background workers) are not available because Neon's storage is remote. The mainstream extensions (pgvector, PostGIS, pg_stat_statements, pgcrypto, etc.) all work.

faqs.question: Doesn't scale-to-zero mean unacceptable cold starts?
faqs.answer: Cold starts on Neon are typically 300-500 ms because the compute layer is stateless and only needs to attach to the existing storage. For most B2B SaaS and developer-facing products, that's invisible behind a normal page load. For latency-critical user-facing endpoints, you can either disable scale-to-zero on the production branch (paid plans) or keep a synthetic ping warming the endpoint.

faqs.question: If I'm already on Supabase, is migrating to Neon hard?
faqs.answer: The database side is straightforward: pg_dump from Supabase, pg_restore into Neon, repoint your connection string. The harder part is the auth/storage/realtime layers, which are Supabase-specific. Each now has a Neon counterpart you can move to at your own pace: Managed Better Auth for auth, S3-compatible Object Storage for files, Functions for Edge Functions, and Realtime (public beta) for subscriptions. Or keep Supabase for some of them and use Neon as the application database.

faqs.question: Does Supabase support branching the same way Neon does?
faqs.answer: Supabase has branching, but the implementation is different. Branching 2.0 (mid-2025) dropped the original Git requirement, so you can create branches from the dashboard, CLI, or API, and Git-less branching became the default in May 2026. A branch is still a brand-new Postgres instance that copies your schema, functions, and config, optionally seeded by a script. Useful for staging and CI on schema changes, but it isn't a copy of production data. Neon's branches share storage pages with the parent, include the full parent dataset, and only diverge on writes.

faqs.question: What about Postgres extensions for AI workloads like pgvector, pgrag, and pg_search?
faqs.answer: Both platforms support pgvector with HNSW indexing. Neon additionally ships pgrag (Neon's own RAG-pipeline extension, still experimental and gated behind an unstable-extensions flag) and is typically faster to add new versions of pgvector because the storage engine isolation makes upgrades safer. Supabase's pgvector support is mature and well-documented for application-layer integrations through its SDKs.

faqs.question: How do the free tiers actually compare in practice?
faqs.answer: Neon's Free plan gives you up to 100 projects, each with 100 CU-hours per month and 1 GB of Postgres storage (up from 0.5 GB on 2 October 2026, 20 GB across all projects), plus Managed Better Auth up to 60K MAU, 5 GB of Object Storage, and Functions with 1M invocations per project. Free databases scale to zero after 5 minutes of inactivity (you can't disable that on the free plan), but they wake automatically on the next connection in well under a second. Supabase's free tier gives you 500 MB database, 1 GB storage, 50K MAUs, 500K edge function calls across a maximum of 2 active projects, but pauses any project after 7 days of inactivity, and a paused project stays down until you restore it from the dashboard. For a side project that gets traffic in fits and starts, Neon's behavior is more forgiving: idle costs nothing and recovery is automatic. (Both free plans verified on 23 November 2026 against neon.com/pricing and supabase.com/pricing.)

faqs.question: Which one has better tooling for AI agents and Cursor/Claude Code workflows?
faqs.answer: Both ship official MCP servers now. Neon's pairs with a clean management API, account-free Claimable Neon databases, an AI Gateway behind one credential, and a branching model that maps naturally to agent reset-state semantics: spawn a branch, run experiment, drop branch. Supabase's MCP server exposes schema and SQL access, and you can even host your own MCP servers on Edge Functions, but provisioning a fresh environment still means standing up a project or branch instance, which is a slower loop than Neon's millisecond copy-on-write branches.

faqs.question: Doesn't Supabase have an auth advantage that Neon can't match?
faqs.answer: Not the way it used to. Managed Better Auth, Neon's auth built on Better Auth (it replaced the earlier Stack Auth-based Neon Auth, which no longer takes new users), went generally available in September 2026: users, sessions, and configuration land in the neon_auth schema and are queryable like any other Postgres data, RLS policies work out of the box, and every database branch gets its own isolated auth environment. It is included up to 1M monthly active users per project on paid plans, where Supabase Pro bills $0.00325 per MAU above 100K. Supabase Auth has the longer track record and a broad provider list (SAML SSO and phone login among them), so check the providers you need, but the 'Neon doesn't do auth' framing no longer holds.

decisionMatrix.criteria: You want a Postgres database that scales to zero when idle and bills only for actual usage
You want auth, storage, and functions bundled with the database, and branched with it for every preview
You run preview environments per pull request with full production-like data
You're building a product that lives or dies on row-level WebSocket subscriptions
Your workload is bursty with long idle stretches (background workers, weekly batch jobs, RAG pipelines)
You want the broadest Postgres major version coverage and to choose your version per project
You want the longest-running bundled backend, with mature mobile SDKs and Realtime out of beta
You're migrating from RDS or self-managed Postgres and want minimal application changes

verdict.summary: Neon and Supabase both bundle a backend around Postgres now, and they build it differently. Neon is a complete backend built on Lakebase Postgres: branching, autoscaling, and scale-to-zero are baked into the storage layer, the wire-protocol contract is plain Postgres, and Managed Better Auth, Object Storage, and Functions branch with the database. Supabase is a backend-as-a-service built around a dedicated Postgres instance, with a longer-running bundle of auth, realtime, storage, and edge functions. The choice comes down to whether you want a backend that branches and scales to zero, or the more established bundle and its mobile SDKs.
verdict.recommendation: Choose Neon for serverless apps, preview environments that need a full copy of the backend, agent-driven test loops, bursty RAG workloads, apps that will grow past 100K monthly active users, and migrations away from RDS. Choose Supabase for mobile-first products, products built on heavy realtime subscriptions, and internal tools that want instant GraphQL and generated types.
